claims.text: Retention of toughness in high-entropy alloys is governed by the stability of ductile grain-boundary complexions.
Adding 1 at.% B promotes thin amorphous intergranular films.
Amorphous intergranular films absorb deformation energy.
Amorphous intergranular films blunt crack tips and thereby delay crack initiation and propagation.
Controlled alloying and homogenization will drive B segregation to grain boundaries in the selected high-entropy alloy.
B-enriched amorphous or complex intergranular films will develop along the grain boundaries.
B segregation promotes formation of ductile intergranular films.
The intergranular films impede crack nucleation and propagation through local deformation absorption and crack-tip blunting.
The B-doped alloy will have higher fracture toughness, Charpy impact energy, and fracture strain than the B-free baseline.
The B-doped alloy will contain thicker, more continuous, and more chemically enriched grain-boundary complexions than the baseline.
Under otherwise identical processing, the B-free baseline has less stable and thinner grain-boundary complexions.
The less stable and thinner grain-boundary complexions in the B-free baseline lead to lower toughness.

The proposed behavior should hold in high-entropy alloys, including suitable FCC alloys, whose processing permits complexion transitions and whose microstructures have substantial grain-boundary density.
The proposed behavior may fail in coarse-grained materials with low grain-boundary area.
The proposed behavior may fail when excessive dopant levels produce brittle secondary phases.
The optimal B segregation concentration is uncertain.
Whether the relevant grain-boundary complexions are amorphous or ordered is uncertain.
Interactions with other alloying elements or impurities may alter the effectiveness of B in stabilizing grain-boundary complexions.
